name: Sage (Salvia officinalis)
short: Essential oils (sage among 4 named) caused convulsions (case reports); rodents given thujone, an oil component, had seizures, deaths and male-rat cancers. Angioedema after sage tea (case report).
text: The most serious harms reported concern sage essential oil and its component thujone, but a child was also admitted with an allergic reaction (angioedema) after drinking sage tea (case report). Commercial essential oils of sage, hyssop, thuja and cedar caused poisoning in eight people, with tonic-clonic convulsions as the main symptom (case reports; the abstract does not say how many involved sage); in the same report's experiments in rats, commercial sage oil caused convulsions of central nervous system origin that became lethal at high doses (the abstract does not give the route), and the authors wrote that the toxicity appeared to be related to camphor in commercial sage oil (camphor and thujone in Dalmatian sage oil). A 1999 case report describes two adults with a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure, whose outcome was good, and a child with generalised tonic status (a form of status epilepticus), whose course was less favourable, after essential oils were absorbed for therapeutic purposes; it cites a literature survey listing sage oil among 11 plant oils that are powerful convulsants (the abstract does not say which oils those patients used). In a two-year animal study, thujone, a component of sage essential oil, given by stomach tube caused seizures in almost all rats and mice at the highest doses; all rats and all female mice at the top doses died before the end of the study; thujone caused cancers of the preputial gland in male rats, and a slight increase in adrenal gland tumours (pheochromocytomas) in male rats may have been related to it, with no increase in cancer in female rats or in mice. A case report describes a 13-year-old boy with an allergy to several plants of the mint family (sage, mint and oregano) who developed angioedema (swelling) after drinking sage tea and again during a supervised sage food challenge. In contrast, trials of sage preparations reported few problems: in a 4-month randomised, placebo-controlled trial of sage extract drops in 42 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease (the abstract does not state the route), side effects did not differ significantly between groups, a meta-analysis of three trials in people with diabetes found no specific side effects reported (the abstract does not state the form or route), and an open, uncontrolled 8-week trial of a once-daily fresh sage leaf tablet in 71 menopausal women called it very well tolerated. The diabetes meta-analysis also found that sage lowered fasting blood sugar and HbA1c. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
